decisiones.pregunta: Tibial plateau · Schatzker as modified by Kfuri: which type?
decisiones.ayuda: It is the language in which the plateau is discussed and it points to the implant: types I-III are lateral, type IV is medial and carries a different prognosis, and V-VI separate the block from the shaft. Kfuri's modification completes the type with the quadrant involved, which is what Schatzker alone does not say: that is why the two questions go together.

reglas.texto: Schatzker as modified by Kfuri I · Pure lateral split — A lateral wedge with no depression. Hueso joven y denso
Schatzker as modified by Kfuri II · Lateral split-depression — The commonest pattern. It demands elevating the depression and filling the defect
Schatzker as modified by Kfuri III · Pure lateral depression — No split line: ligamentotaxis does not lift it. Elevation through a metaphyseal window and grafting
Schatzker as modified by Kfuri IV · Medial plateau — The medial plateau carries most of the load: worse prognosis. It may be a reduced knee dislocation: exclude peroneal nerve and vascular injury
Schatzker as modified by Kfuri V · Bicondylar — Both plateaus, with the shaft still in continuity
Schatzker as modified by Kfuri VI · Bicondylar with metaphyseal-diaphyseal dissociation — The articular block is separated from the shaft: that is two zones. Partes blandas casi siempre comprometidas
Schatzker as modified by Kfuri · quadrants Anterolateral — The classic quadrant of the lateral split-depression. Reached through the lateral approach, with the patient supine
Schatzker as modified by Kfuri · quadrants Anteromedial — Depression or split of the anterior half of the medial plateau. Reached through the medial approach; the lateral plate does not hold it

Schatzker as modified by Kfuri · quadrants Posterolateral — The hardest to reach: it lies behind the fibula and below the common peroneal nerve. A pure depression the AP radiograph does not show: it needs CT

Schatzker as modified by Kfuri · quadrants Posteromedial — It is the fragment most often forgotten and the one that most often fails. It subluxes in flexion: neither the lateral nor the anteromedial plate controls it
Garden Undisplaced · Garden I-II — Valgus impacted or complete without displacement. In situ fixation with screws or a sliding hip screw
Garden Displaced · Garden III-IV — Trabeculae broken or discontinuous. High risk of necrosis and non-union
Pauwels III · more than 50° — An almost vertical line: the load shears instead of compressing. Parallel screws then work in shear and give way
Neer 1 part · undisplaced — No fragment exceeds 1 cm or 45°. Tratamiento casi siempre conservador
Neer 2 parts · greater tuberosity — Eccentric pull of the cuff: a tension band setting. A lower surgical threshold in the active patient, around 5 mm
Neer 3 parts — Head, one tuberosity and shaft
Neer 4 parts — High risk of head necrosis. Consider reverse arthroplasty in the older patient
Neer Fracture-dislocation — The head is out of the glenoid: a relative emergency
Hertel · predictors of ischaemia Metaphyseal head extension shorter than 8 mm — It is the strongest predictor of ischaemia. It is measured at the calcar, on the head fragment
Hertel · predictors of ischaemia Medial hinge disrupted, displaced more than 2 mm — Without a medial hinge there is no supply from the anterior circumflex artery
Hertel · predictors of ischaemia Basicervical fracture line — It cuts the supply to the head below the anatomical neck
Hawkins II · With subtalar subluxation or dislocation — Risk of 20 to 50%
Hawkins III · Subtalar and tibiotalar dislocation — Risk above 80%. The body is extruded: urgent reduction, and watch the skin
Hawkins IV · Adds talonavicular dislocation — Necrosis is virtually certain
Sanders III · Three fragments — Two fracture lines, with a depressed central fragment
Sanders IV · Four or more fragments — Comminution of the posterior facet. Worse functional prognosis: consider primary subtalar arthrodesis
Letournel and Judet Posterior wall — The commonest. Kocher-Langenbeck, en prono o lateral
Letournel and Judet Posterior column — Kocher-Langenbeck
Letournel and Judet Anterior wall — Ilioinguinal or anterior intrapelvic, supine
Letournel and Judet Anterior column — Ilioinguinal or anterior intrapelvic
Letournel and Judet Transverse — It separates the acetabulum into upper and lower halves. Puede exigir abordaje combinado o extensible
Letournel and Judet T-shaped — Transverse plus a vertical line. One of the hardest: almost always two windows
Letournel and Judet Posterior column with posterior wall — Kocher-Langenbeck; check the sciatic nerve from the start
Letournel and Judet Transverse with posterior wall — The commonest associated pattern
Letournel and Judet Anterior column with posterior hemitransverse — Usually through an anterior route, with indirect control of the posterior one
Letournel and Judet Both-column — No articular fragment stays attached to the axial skeleton. The spur sign on the obturator oblique confirms it
Young and Burgess Lateral compression II — It adds a bucket-handle fracture of the iliac wing
Young and Burgess Lateral compression III · windswept — Lateral compression on one side and opening on the other. Mortalidad alta
Young and Burgess Anteroposterior compression II · open book — Diastasis over 2.5 cm with the anterior sacroiliac ligaments torn. It increases the pelvic volume: urgent binder or external fixator
Young and Burgess Anteroposterior compression III — Complete dissociation of the hemipelvis. The pattern that bleeds and transfuses most
Young and Burgess Vertical shear — Cranial displacement of the hemipelvis. Vertical instability: a binder does not control it
Young and Burgess Combined mechanism — Mixed patterns, usually from a fall from height
Tile · AO pelvis B · Rotationally unstable, vertically stable — Open book or lateral compression. Anterior fixation is usually enough
Tile · AO pelvis C · Rotationally and vertically unstable — Complete disruption of the posterior complex. It demands posterior fixation: iliosacral screws or a plate
Vancouver B1 · Around the stem, stem well fixed — Fixation with a locked plate, cables or a combination
Vancouver B2 · Stem loose, adequate bone stock — The operation is to revise the stem, not to fix the fracture. Putting a plate over a loose stem is guaranteed failure
Vancouver B3 · Stem loose and poor bone stock — Revision with a long stem, allograft or megaprosthesis
Vancouver C · Distal to the tip of the stem — It is treated as a distal femoral fracture. Beware of the zone between implants: overlap the plate with the stem
Winquist and Hansen 0 · No comminution — Trazo simple, contacto cortical completo
Winquist and Hansen I · Small fragment — Less than 25% of the circumference. It still shares load
Winquist and Hansen II · Between 25 and 50% — Enough contact to tolerate dynamisation
Winquist and Hansen III · More than 50% — There is no column left to share load. Static locking is mandatory
Winquist and Hansen IV · Segmental, no cortical contact — The nail carries the whole load. Length and rotation depend entirely on the bolts
Mason III · Comminuted — Not reconstructable: consider a radial head replacement. Isolated excision is contraindicated if there is instability
Mason IV · With elbow dislocation — Look for the terrible triad: coronoid and lateral collateral ligament. The radial head is a secondary stabiliser that here becomes primary
Lauge-Hansen Supination-adduction — Transverse fibular line below the syndesmosis. Vertical line of the medial malleolus: it calls for a buttress, not friction screws
Lauge-Hansen Supination-external rotation — The commonest pattern. Spiral fibular line at the level of the syndesmosis
Lauge-Hansen Pronation-abduction — Comminuted lateral fibula, above the syndesmosis. Transverse avulsion line of the medial malleolus
Lauge-Hansen Pronation-external rotation — High fibula: rule out a Maisonneuve by palpating the whole fibula. Sindesmosis casi siempre lesionada
